spans.note: document title and Executive Summary heading

spans.assertion: the analysis tested whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, using 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain) in the 2012-2013 season
the adjusted risk difference was 0.280 percentage points (95% CI -0.003 to 0.606, p=0.112)
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.239 (95% CI 0.951 to 1.614, p=0.112)
the overall conclusion reached was that the discrimination hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
the point estimate suggests a small positive association, with dark-skinned players having 0.28 percentage points higher probability of receiving a red card
the 95% CI includes zero and p=0.112 exceeds the conventional α=0.05 threshold, so the evidence is insufficient to conclude referees discriminate based on skin tone

spans.note: '1. Primary Estimand: Adjusted Risk Difference' heading

spans.assertion: the risk difference (dark vs light) was 0.280 percentage points
the 95% confidence interval for the risk difference was [-0.003, 0.606]
the two-sided p-value was 0.1120, evaluated against α=0.05
the risk difference was adjusted for position, league country, height, weight, age, and number of games played
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.280 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players
the 95% CI crosses zero (barely including negative values), indicating the difference is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level
the risk difference was estimated via marginal standardization (g-computation) from a logistic regression model
confidence intervals were computed using a player-level cluster bootstrap with 1,000 iterations

spans.note: '2. Secondary Estimand: Adjusted Odds Ratio' heading

spans.assertion: the odds ratio (dark vs light) was 1.239
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was [0.951, 1.614]
the two-sided p-value for the odds ratio was 0.1120
the odds of receiving a red card are 23.9% higher for dark-skinned players after adjustment
the 95% CI includes 1.0, consistent with no association

spans.note: 'Unit of Analysis and Sample Size' heading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad
there were 42,979 dyads after exclusions
there were 547 unique players in the sample
there were 2,335 unique referees in the sample
546 dyads had at least one red card event
skin tone was independently rated by two blind raters on a 5-point scale (0=very light to 1=very dark) from player profile photos
dark skin was defined as an average rating of 0.75 or above
the dark-skin group comprised 7,065 dyads and 94 unique players
light skin was defined as an average rating of 0.25 or below
the light-skin group comprised 35,914 dyads and 453 unique players
middle skin-tone categories (0.375-0.625) were excluded to create clear contrast groups
inter-rater reliability between the two skin-tone raters was Pearson r=0.923
red card receipt was defined as a binary indicator (anyRedCard=1 if redCards>0) across all encounters between a player and referee
the unadjusted red card rate was 1.21% for light-skinned and 1.56% for dark-skinned players
all continuous covariates were standardized (mean-centered, SD=1) before modeling
position (Defender as reference, plus Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Unknown) was included as a covariate
position distribution differed by skin tone, with 44% of dark-skinned dyads at forward vs 19% of light-skinned dyads
league country (England as reference, plus France, Germany, Spain) was included as a covariate
red card rates varied by league, 0.86% in Germany vs 1.67% in France
height (continuous, cm, standardized) was included as a covariate

spans.note: stated rationale that player physicality may correlate with aggressive play

spans.assertion: weight (continuous, kg, standardized) was included as a covariate

spans.note: stated rationale that heavier players may play more physically

spans.assertion: age (continuous, years, calculated from birth year assuming a 2012.5 season midpoint) was included as a covariate

spans.note: stated rationale that experience may affect play style and referee perception

spans.assertion: number of games in the player-referee dyad (standardized) was included as a covariate

spans.note: stated rationale that more games means more exposure/opportunity for red cards

spans.assertion: 21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no player photo available)
64,627 dyads were excluded for missing age data, since birth date was unavailable and age was treated as an important confounder
370 dyads with missing height/weight were imputed with median values
the final analytic sample was 42,979 dyads, 29.4% of the original dataset
a logistic regression model was used with the binary outcome anyRedCard
the model was specified as logit(P(Red Card)) on dark-skin indicator, height, weight, age, games, position dummies, and league dummies
cluster-robust standard errors at the player level were used
there was a mean of 78.6 dyads per player

spans.note: rationale that clustering accounts for within-player correlation across referees

spans.assertion: the logistic model was fit to obtain coefficients
P(red card | dark=1) was predicted for all observations
P(red card | dark=0) was predicted for all observations
the risk difference was computed as the mean predicted probability under dark=1 minus under dark=0
the 95% CI was computed via player-level cluster bootstrap, resampling 547 players with replacement and refitting the model 1,000 times
continuous predictors were standardized (mean=0, SD=1) for numerical stability
no transformations were applied to the outcome
no survey weights or inverse probability weights were applied; all dyads were weighted equally
player fixed effects were not used; player-level clustering via robust SEs was preferred instead
skin tone is a player-level characteristic with no within-player variation
fixed effects would not be identified for the main effect of interest
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is NOT SUPPORTED by the data
the p-value (0.112) exceeds α=0.05, so the null hypothesis of no difference is not rejected
the 95% CI [-0.003, 0.606] includes zero (barely), so the true risk difference could plausibly be zero or slightly favor light-skinned players
the point estimate (0.28pp) with a wide CI spanning 0.61pp reflects substantial uncertainty, and its upper/lower bounds imply materially different conclusions
the baseline red card rate is low (1.27% overall) and a 0.28pp increase represents a 22% relative increase, which would be meaningful if robust
given the uncertainty, the estimate cannot be distinguished from no effect
in the full dataset with age imputed (N=107,606), the risk difference was 0.229pp with p=0.052
using continuous skin tone, a 2-SD increase corresponded to a risk difference of 0.181pp with p=0.146
all specifications yield non-significant results at α=0.05, though the full dataset analysis approaches significance
the data do not provide statistically significant evidence that referees discriminate against dark-skinned players after adjustment
point estimates consistently show a small positive association, but confidence intervals are too wide to rule out chance
14.7% of dyads lack skin tone ratings due to no available photo
60% of dyads with skin tone data lack age data
the final sample represents only 29% of the original dyads

spans.note: caveat that players with complete data may differ systematically, potentially biasing estimates
caveat that ratings were based on 2D photos, not in-person assessment
caveat that lighting, image quality, and photo angle may introduce measurement error

spans.assertion: dichotomizing skin tone into dark vs light discards information from the middle categories
classification error in skin tone would bias estimates toward the null (non-differential misclassification)
dyad-level analysis creates clustering by both player and referee
only player clustering was adjusted for; referee clustering was not addressed, which could underestimate standard errors
an alternative player-level-only analysis was not pursued because it would lose referee heterogeneity information
play style/aggressiveness was not measured or adjusted for, though it could confound the skin-tone effect if correlated with it
finer position distinctions (e.g., defensive vs attacking midfielder) were not captured
club or team quality was not adjusted for
referee implicit bias scores were not used in the primary model due to high missingness
only country-level implicit bias scores were available for referees
opponent strength and game context data were not available and not used
red cards were aggregated across the entire career of encounters between a player and referee
the analysis could not assess whether discrimination varies over time or by game situation
the model assumed a linear relationship between log-odds and continuous predictors, which appeared reasonable
interactions between skin tone and other covariates were not comprehensively tested; no interactions were assumed
player-level clustering was assumed to capture the dependence structure
referee-level clustering was ignored, which could underestimate uncertainty

spans.note: caveat that bootstrap resamples may not represent the population if players are non-exchangeable

spans.assertion: the complete-case analysis assumed data were missing at random conditional on observed covariates

spans.note: caveat that estimates could be biased if missingness depends on unobserved factors

spans.assertion: the analysis required overlap in covariate distributions between the dark and light skin-tone groups
position distribution differed substantially between groups (44% forwards among dark vs 19% among light)

spans.note: caveat that the model extrapolates for dark-skinned players in positions rare among that group
'Key Assumptions That Could Not Be Fully Met' heading

spans.assertion: the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption was likely violated, since play style, reputation, and team context are plausible unavailable confounders
exchangeability of players may be violated if star players differ from bench players in both discrimination exposure and data completeness
clustering was only done by player, not by referee, potentially understating uncertainty
the sample was restricted to players with photos and complete covariate data

spans.note: caveat that the sample may overrepresent established players, direction of bias unknown

spans.assertion: skin tone classification error is present as a source of measurement bias
the direction of measurement bias is likely toward the null (non-differential)
unmeasured play style differences remain a source of confounding bias

spans.note: caveat that confounding bias direction could go toward or away from null depending on correlation structure

spans.assertion: interaction effects were ignored in the model
non-linear relationships were not explored

spans.note: caveat that direction of misspecification bias is unknown

spans.assertion: the sample was large: 42,979 dyads, 547 players, 2,335 referees
exposure measurement was high quality due to blind dual raters and high inter-rater reliability (r=0.92)
inference used player-clustered SEs and cluster bootstrap for the primary estimand, providing robustness
covariate adjustment was comprehensive, covering position, league, physical characteristics, and exposure (games)
dichotomization of skin tone into dark vs light was a clear, transparent operational definition
multiple sensitivity analyses showed results consistent across specifications
N dyads were 35,914 for light skin and 7,065 for dark skin
N players were 453 for light skin and 94 for dark skin
red card counts were 436 for light skin and 110 for dark skin
red card rate was 1.21% for light skin and 1.56% for dark skin

total games were 109,458 for light skin and 20,914 for dark skin

average weight was 76.3kg for light skin and 76.7kg for dark skin

Goalkeeper share was 11.3% light skin vs 1.8% dark skin
Midfielder share was 37.3% light skin vs 24.1% dark skin
Unknown position share was 5.9% light skin vs 7.9% dark skin
dark-skinned players disproportionately play forward, a lower baseline red-card-rate position than defender, which partly explains why the adjusted effect is smaller than the crude effect
the crude (unadjusted) risk difference was 0.34 percentage points
England share was 23.9% light skin vs 39.0% dark skin
France share was 14.5% light skin vs 29.1% dark skin
Germany share was 36.2% light skin vs 16.5% dark skin
Spain share was 25.4% light skin vs 15.4% dark skin
the dark-skin coefficient was 0.215 (SE 0.135, p=0.112)

model diagnostics showed Pseudo R²=0.072 and AUC=0.742, described as fair discrimination
the primary complete-case analysis (N=42,979) yielded RD=0.280pp, p=0.112, OR=1.239
sensitivity analysis 1 (age imputed, N=107,606) yielded RD=0.229pp, p=0.052, OR=1.198
sensitivity analysis 2 (continuous skin tone, N=42,979) yielded RD=0.181pp per 2-SD change, p=0.146, OR not applicable
all analyses yield non-significant results at α=0.05, with the full dataset approaching borderline significance (p=0.052)

the analysis is fully reproducible using the provided Python script, which performs data loading/preprocessing, descriptive statistics, logistic regression with clustered SEs, marginal standardization, cluster bootstrap, and sensitivity analyses
the analysis used Python 3.11, pandas 2.1.0, statsmodels 0.14.0, numpy 1.25.2, and scikit-learn 1.3.0
the data came from /workspace/data/soccer/soccer.csv, containing 146,028 rows and 28 columns
